The diagram shown above is the slope field for which of the following differential equations?
worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14040443/assets/1e37d101f131279fc198fd97f03e6a35e15bc2d62622e1730aadbc316dc8d0bf.png)

 

Notice the following properties of the given slope field:

- First, the slopes of the slope field are horizontal along the lines $y=-2$ and $y=0.$ Therefore, the right-hand side of the differential equation should equal zero on both of these lines.

Of the given equations, the only equations that satisfy this condition are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-\frac{1}{2}y(y+2)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}y(y+2)^{2} \\ {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}(y+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Second, the lines $y=-2$ and $y=0$ divide the plane into $3$ regions. The sign of the slopes in each of the $3$ regions are easily deduced by considering the behavior of the solution curves in these regions. This information is summarized in the following table:

| Region | $y<-2$ | $-2<y<0$ | $y>0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Slope | $↗$ | $↗$ | $↘$ |
| Sign | $+$ | $+$ | $-$ |

Of the remaining options, the only one that gives this behavior is

$$
{y}^{′}=-\frac{1}{2}y(y+2)^{2}.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is ${y}^{′}=-\frac{1}{2}y(y+2)^{2}.$
